source.title: On the Implicit Flatness Bias of Sharpness-Aware Minimization: A Linear Stability Analysis with Quantitative Hyperparameter Bounds

record.file_problem: The supplied paper text is complete; some figure and table content is flattened.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests associations between SAM hyperparameters, Hessian sharpness, and test accuracy using correlations and controlled experiments. It does not test the claim versions’ specified memorization, optimizer, batch-size, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or example-removal effects.
record.gate_note: The reported correlations between perturbation radius and largest Hessian eigenvalue measure sharpness, not the train–test gap. The pooled hyperparameter correlation is with peak test accuracy, not the gap. Table 3 compares reported test accuracies for SAM variants and SGD. Cited prior findings are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study tests SAM's radius–Hessian relationship, not any listed claim version. Its unscaled largest Hessian eigenvalue and peak test accuracy do not measure V7's magnitude-aware sharpness or train–test gap. Batch-size settings and pooled correlations do not establish V5's isolated fixed-epoch batch-size effect. SAM and TLC-SAM comparisons do not test V4's adaptive-gradient optimizer claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but incomplete. Under local linearization, squared-loss, near-interpolation, and noise-alignment assumptions, the authors derive a cubic bound on stable SAM solutions' largest Hessian eigenvalue. Their experiments largely support the negative radius–curvature association, while excessive radius can harm accuracy. They also conclude that locality-controlled radius adaptation further suppresses the top eigenvalue and generally improves fixed-radius SAM's test accuracy; the analysis does not cover the full training trajectory.
record.recipe_differences: Studies SAM radius and Taylor-locality adaptation using a local linear-stability analysis and CIFAR experiments; it does not reproduce the original claim's interventions or measures.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported ρ–Hessian association varies in strength with architecture, batch size, and learning rate; one VGG-19 setting is nonsignificant. The paper also cautions that accuracy can deteriorate when ρ is overly large.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger SAM radius correlates negatively with the largest Hessian eigenvalue in all 25 ResNet-18 settings and significantly in 24 of 25 VGG-19 settings.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAM's perturbation radius is associated with lower unscaled maximum Hessian curvature across the tested CIFAR-100 settings.

fits_no_version.finding: The cube-root hyperparameter factor correlates positively with peak test accuracy: SCC 0.905 for ResNet-18 and 0.907 for VGG-19.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The pooled factor (b/(2ρη²))^(1/3) ranks peak test accuracy in these SAM experiments; individual hyperparameter effects remain unidentified.

fits_no_version.finding: SAM has higher reported test accuracy than SGD in all six architecture–dataset comparisons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAM outperforms SGD on the tested CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 benchmarks under the authors' implementation.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing radius can lower maximum Hessian curvature while test accuracy deteriorates when radius becomes excessive.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Lower unscaled maximum Hessian curvature alone does not guarantee better test accuracy across SAM radius choices.

record.problems: The authors note that the analysis is local, assumes linearization near an interpolating minimum and squared loss, and does not cover the full training trajectory. The pooled accuracy association varies batch size, learning rate, and radius simultaneously, so it cannot isolate their effects. One VGG-19 correlation is nonsignificant; authors attribute it to an anomalous Hessian estimate. Table 3 includes comparisons drawn from different sources and is not intended as a strict ranking. Table 1 is flattened in the supplied text, preventing recovery of several cells.
record.rows_left_out: Within the 60-row cap, the six reported SGD-versus-SAM accuracy comparisons in Table 3 are not all extractable: only ResNet-18 and WideResNet-28-10 and PyramidNet-110 comparisons are included here, while rows for other SAM variants are omitted because they compare methods outside the claim versions. The supplementary-material TLC-controlled Eigen-SAM values are mentioned in text but omitted to prioritize the main tabulated results.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label generalization, and chance-level random-label test accuracy.
Width increases beyond interpolation and their test-error effects.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and local-connectivity explanations.
Adaptive-gradient methods versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Held-out performance differences attributable to batch size under fixed epochs, and recovery through adapted recipes.
Dropout effects, underfitting, training-set size, and augmentation interactions.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance versus train–test gaps at similarly low training loss, including rankings against norm and margin measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All rows remain unlinked to V1–V8. Their cannot_determine states concern those versions, not whether the paper's separate numerical findings exist. Table 1's flattened text preserves the previously omitted ResNet-18 cells. No omitted result establishes a listed version; the unscaled-curvature/accuracy trade-off does not directly challenge magnitude-aware V7.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence; random-label test accuracy.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation and their effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum under different tuning and regularization recipes.
Large-batch versus small-batch generalization under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Dropout effects and interactions with data augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness, train–test gaps at similarly low training loss, and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.
